The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Struggles with Fame and Addiction (2005 onwards)
podcast.body: Starting around 2005, Amy Winehouse became increasingly jaded and angry with fame, which was accompanied by extensive media coverage of her heavy drinking and drug use. "Starting in about 2005, a lot of media attention was focused on her drinking and heavy drug use."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hospitalization for Overdose (Summer 2007)
podcast.body: In the summer of 2007, Winehouse was hospitalized following an overdose involving a combination of heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, ketamine, and alcohol. "Sometime in the summer of 2007, she was admitted to the hospital, suffering from an overdose of heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, ketamine, and alcohol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cause of Death (2011)
podcast.body: The medical examiner ruled Amy Winehouse's death as "death by misadventure." She had consumed so much alcohol that she passed out, went into respiratory arrest, and fell into a coma. Her blood alcohol level was 0.416, which is more than five times the legal limit for driving. Her death was attributed to alcohol toxicity. Although she had gone to rehab, it "obviously didn't help." "The medical examiner called this a death by misadventure. She drank so much that she passed out, went into respiratory arrest, and fell into a coma."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death by Alcohol Toxicity (July 23, 2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse died tragically at age 27 on July 23, 2011, from alcohol toxicity, officially ruled a "death by misadventure." Her blood alcohol level was 0.416, more than five times the legal limit for driving, leading her to pass out, go into respiratory arrest, and fall into a coma. She was a deeply troubled woman, struggling with alcoholism, bulimia, and drug addiction. She had been diagnosed with emphysema in her mid-20s from crack cocaine use, leaving her lungs operating at only 70% capacity. She also had an irregular heartbeat, severe nicotine dependency, and recurring chest infections. In her final hours on July 22, 2011, she was in her Camden Square, London bedroom watching YouTube videos of herself and drinking heavily, after a two-week period of abstinence. Her live-in bodyguard, Andrew Morris, found her unresponsive the next afternoon. "Her blood alcohol level was 0.416. More than five times the legal limit for driving. Basically, she died of alcohol toxicity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death in London Flat (July 23, 2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse was discovered deceased in her flat in Camden, North London, on July 23, 2011. Her death, while shocking, was not entirely unexpected given her recent struggles. "Amy Winehouse was found dead on July 23, 2011 in her flat in Camden in North London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Erratic Performances and Canceled Tour (2011)
podcast.body: Winehouse's performances became increasingly unpredictable, culminating in a particularly poor gig in front of 20,000 people in Belgrade, Serbia, which led to the cancellation of a planned European comeback tour. At the time, she was supposed to be taking Liberium, a medication for alcohol and anxiety, but she expressed boredom and unwillingness to follow medical advice. "After a particularly bad gig in front of about 20,000 people in Belgrade, Serbia, a European tour designed as a big comeback for her was canceled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Days and Alcohol Relapse (2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse was living at her home in Camden Square, London. On July 20th, 2011, her live-in bodyguard, Andrew Morris, joined her, tasked with keeping an eye on her. Over the next couple of days, Morris observed her drinking moderately, mostly vodka. By the evening of July 22nd, she had broken a period of abstinence and had been drinking "pretty hard" over the preceding two weeks, though Andrew Morris noted she seemed "fine" and her "usual bubbly self." "On July 20th, 2011, she was joined by her live in Bodyguard, guy with the name of Andrew Morris, who was supposed to keep an eye on her."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Days and Discovery of Death (July 20-23, 2011)
podcast.body: On July 20, 2011, her bodyguard found her appearing drunk, a relapse after a period of sobriety, and stayed with her. On the night of July 22, she was observed watching YouTube videos of her past gigs, laughing until 2 AM. The next morning, July 23, her bodyguard checked on her at 10 AM, finding her seemingly asleep. However, when he checked again at 3 PM, she was not breathing and had no pulse. Ambulances arrived at 3:54 PM, and she was declared dead shortly thereafter. "On the night of July 22, Amy stayed up late, watching YouTube videos of some of her past gigs. She seemed fine, laughing until about two in the morning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Days with Bodyguard (July 20-23, 2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse spent her final days at her home in Camden Square, London, under the observation of her live-in bodyguard, Andrew Morris, who was tasked with keeping an eye on her. From July 20 to 22, Morris observed her engaging in "moderate drinking," mostly vodka. On the evening of July 22, her last hours were spent in her bedroom, watching YouTube videos of herself on her laptop and drinking heavily, despite having abstained for a period before hitting the bottle hard for two weeks. She appeared tipsy but not completely drunk when she briefly showed Morris a YouTube video. Morris checked on her at 2:30 AM on July 23 (she seemed asleep) and again at 10:00 AM (still seemed asleep). By 3:00 PM, he noticed she hadn't moved, and with two empty vodka bottles on the floor, he realized something was wrong, calling an ambulance at 3:54 PM. "Amy came at least once to show Andrew a YouTube video of someone she once dated. She was tipsy, but not completely drunk. That was the last time anybody saw her alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Health Issues and Addictions (Pre-2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse was a deeply troubled woman, struggling with alcoholism, bulimia, and drug addiction. Her heavy crack smoking led to a diagnosis of emphysema in her mid-twenties, with her lungs operating at only 70% capacity, a significant impediment for a singer. She also suffered from an irregular heartbeat and a severe nicotine dependency, which required her to wear nicotine patches, in addition to recurring chest infections. "She was a very troubled woman, an alcoholic, bulimic drug addict. She smoked so much crack that she was diagnosed with emphysema in her mid-twenties."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Last Hours and Discovery (2011)
podcast.body: On the evening of July 22nd, 2011, Amy spent her final hours in her bedroom, watching YouTube videos of herself on her laptop and drinking heavily. She came out at least once to show Morris a YouTube video of someone she had once dated, appearing tipsy but not completely drunk; this was the last time anyone saw her alive. Morris checked on her at 2:30 AM on July 23rd, finding her seemingly asleep, and again at 10 AM, when she appeared normal while sleeping in bed. However, when he returned after 3 PM, she had not moved. Two empty vodka bottles were on the floor, and she was fully clothed. Morris called an ambulance at 3:54 PM, but it was far too late. "Amy's final hours were spent in her bedroom watching YouTube videos of herself on her laptop, and drinking. A lot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relapses and Death (2011)
podcast.body: Despite going to rehab several times, including a two-week stay in late January 2008, Amy Winehouse experienced a major relapse after a brief period of sobriety, which led to her death by alcohol intoxication on July 23rd, 2011. She had been sober for almost two weeks but began drinking again due to boredom, telling her doctor this three days before her death. The coroner's report stated she spent her last hours drinking vodka alone in her bedroom, watching YouTube videos of herself, leading to her stopping breathing, slipping into a coma, and dying with a blood alcohol level 20% above what is usually fatal. Her security guard found her lying face down in her bed at 2:30 AM and she had not moved by 3 PM the following afternoon when paramedics were called. "She drank so much that she stopped breathing and she slipped into a coma and then she died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Severe Health Problems (Mid-2000s - 2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse suffered from a multitude of severe health issues. Diagnosed with emphysema in her mid-20s due to extensive crack cocaine use, her lungs operated at only 70% capacity, a critical condition for a singer. She also had an irregular heartbeat, a serious nicotine dependency requiring patches, and recurring chest infections. These health problems compounded her struggles with alcoholism, bulimia, and drug addiction. "She smoked so much crack that she was diagnosed with emphysema in her mid-20s. Her lungs were operating at 70% capacity at best, which is not a good thing for anyone, let alone a singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tragic Death (July 23, 2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse was found dead by her bodyguard in her London flat at the age of 27. The official verdict was alcohol poisoning, with her blood alcohol content recorded at 0.416, more than four times the legal limit for drunk driving. This combined with her existing health issues, including drug addiction, alcoholism, anorexia, bulimia, emphysema from smoking, and likely mental health issues, proved to be too much for her weakened body. "Amy was found dead by a bodyguard in her London flat on July 23, 2011."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tragic Death at 27 (2011)
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse tragically died at the age of 27. Her passing was the subject of a 2015 documentary titled "Autopsy, the last hours of Amy Winehouse," which explored the circumstances of her final moments. "Amy Winehouse was one of those music personalities who died tragically at age 27. Her death was the subject of a documentary in 2015 called Autopsy, the last hours of Amy Winehouse."

podcast.title: Broad Influence on Contemporary Artists
podcast.body: Her distinctive style and sound have had a profound impact on a wide range of artists across different genres. Influences can be heard in the music of Florence Welch (Florence + The Machine), Lady Gaga, Lana Del Rey, Alessia Cara, and Billie Eilish. Male singers such as Bruno Mars and Sam Smith also credit Amy as an inspiration. "Her influence can be heard in the music of any number of artists. Florence Welch or Florence in the machine. Lady Gaga, Lana Del Rey, Alissa Carrier and Billie Eilish."

podcast.title: Career and Public Persona
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse was celebrated as a once-in-a-generation voice, possessing a distinctive image, look, and feel that garnered both commercial success and critical praise. Beyond her music, she was also recognized as an activist, philanthropist, and successful businesswoman, amassing a fortune of at least 10 million pounds, making her one of the richest British individuals under 30. However, her fame was also fueled by her struggles with drinking, drugs, tumultuous relationships, dysfunctional family dynamics, and self-destructive behavior, which kept her under constant paparazzi scrutiny and widely reported in the British media. "There was no one like Amy out there in the Outs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cause of Death: Alcohol Poisoning
podcast.body: The coroner determined that Amy Winehouse died from acute alcohol poisoning, having consumed an excessive amount of vodka, with two large and one small empty bottles found in her room. Her blood alcohol level was a staggering 0.416, which is five times the legal limit. She was 27 years old at the time of her death. "The corner declared that she died of alcohol poisoning. She'd had too much vodka."

podcast.title: Estimated £500,000 Spent on Drugs Before Death
podcast.body: A report released in 2021 estimated that Amy Winehouse spent approximately £500,000 on drugs before her death at the age of 26. This figure highlights the severe extent of her addiction. "a report came out this year that estimated that Amy Winehouse spent 500,000 pounds on drugs before she died at the age of 26."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Charity Work
podcast.body: Beyond her musical achievements, Amy Winehouse was known for her significant philanthropic contributions. She donated substantial amounts of money to organizations dedicated to children's welfare and the arts community, and actively worked to raise awareness for breast cancer. "Her charity work, for example. Amy gave away a ton of money to organizations concerned with children's welfare. She gave money to the arts community. She worked to raise awareness of breast cancer."

podcast.title: Health Issues
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse struggled with numerous health problems, including bulimia, self-harming, domestic violence issues, public drunkenness, and addiction to various substances like crack, heroin, ketamine, cocaine, and ecstasy. She underwent psychological and psychiatric counseling, and was prescribed drugs for alcohol withdrawal and anxiety. At 24, she was diagnosed with early stage emphysema. "People health problems, bulimia, cutting issues with domestic violence, public drunkenness, crack, heroin, ketamine, coke, ecstasy."

podcast.title: Industry Victim - Unprofitable Rehabilitation
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse is cited as an example of an artist who was not rehabilitated because a "rehabilitated Amy Winehouse" was not considered profitable by the industry. This illustrates the industry's prioritization of quick money over artist well-being, leading to artists becoming "broken toys." "a Amy Wunghaus nos rehabilitaba porque no era rentable una y Wunghaus rehabilitada y esto al final los lleva a tener estos juguetes rotos que acaban así."

podcast.title: Mental Health Diagnoses
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse openly discussed her problems, revealing she was bipolar, depressed, had an eating disorder, and engaged in self-harm. A doctor suggested she might be suffering from borderline personality disorder, leading to reckless behavior, and a specialist recommended dialectical behavior therapy. "When she did open up about her problems a little later, she confessed to being bipolar, depressed, having an eating disorder, and cutting herself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paving the Way for Adele
podcast.body: It is suggested that Amy Winehouse's success and unique sound helped create a more accepting environment for artists like Adele, indicating her significant cultural impact. "And if there hadn't been an Amy Winehouse, the world might not have been so accepting of somebody like Adele, for example."

podcast.title: Personal Act of Philanthropy
podcast.body: While on vacation in St. Lucia, Amy heard about a man in desperate need of surgery. Despite not knowing him personally, she intervened and covered all the expenses for his medical treatment. "When she was on vacation in St. Lucia, she heard of a man who desperately needed surgery. Although she didn't know him, Amy stepped in and paid for everything."

podcast.title: Posthumous Foundation
podcast.body: After her death, her family established the Amy Winehouse Foundation, which is dedicated to supporting young people struggling with drug and alcohol problems, continuing her legacy of care. "And in death, there's an Amy Winehouse foundation which was set up by her family. It's also dedicated to helping young people suffering from drug and alcohol problems."

podcast.title: Public Scandals and Health Decline
podcast.body: Tabloids published pictures of her smoking crack, and she faced allegations of assault, had frequent fights with her husband and father, and was constantly hounded by paparazzi. Her health deteriorated, manifesting as an irregular heartbeat and severely reduced lung capacity (approximately 70%) due to heavy smoking of tobacco and other substances. "The tabloids posted pictures of her smoking crack. There were allegations of assault. There were fights with her husband and her father, and the hounding from the paparazzi was constant."

podcast.title: Untimely Death and Musical Legacy
podcast.body: Amy Winehouse tragically passed away in the summer of 2011 due to alcohol poisoning. Despite her short career, she is credited with almost single-handedly reintroducing a soulful type of R&B to a new generation of listeners. "Now, of course, she's no longer with us having died of alcohol poisoning in the summer of 2011. But when she was still alive, Amy almost single-handedly brought back a soulful type of R&B for a brand new generation."

xref.title: Unique Identity and Influences
xref.body: Halsey has synthesized various influences, including Jagger, Bowie, Amy Winehouse, and Dolores O'Riordan, to craft a distinctive identity. This identity incorporates concepts of gender identity, bisexuality, film noir, mental health, political activism, racial justice, and motherhood, all stemming from an authentic personal place. "Halsey has taken a bunch of different influences from Jagger and Bowie to Amy Winehouse and Dolores are reared in and crafted a unique identity that also includes concepts of gender identity, bisexuality, film noir, mental health, political activism, racial justice, motherhood, and so much more."
